zones.notes: Full floor coverage for overhead spray. Overspray from ceiling work falls straight down — entire floor below the ceiling work area must be covered. Canvas drop cloths or builder's paper. Significantly more floor coverage than wood wall work (which only needs perimeter drops).

Perimeter drop cloths for brush drip protection. Less overspray risk than spray — drips fall from overhead brush work but contained to area directly below worker position. Drop cloth runners along work path.

zones.upgrade_scenario: Upgrades to full_mask when wall below is SS_PAINTED_*
zones.notes: Upper wall band masking near ceiling for overspray containment during spray. Paper/plastic film at wall-ceiling junction area extending 12-24 inches down wall. Key distinction from SF_WOOD_WALL_NC which uses ceiling_line zone (masking ceiling above). Here we mask the wall BELOW the ceiling.

Mask ceiling-mounted lights, fans, smoke detectors, sprinkler heads. Always required regardless of application method — fixtures are embedded in the ceiling surface being painted. Tape and plastic bag or masking film over each fixture.
Lightweight plastic pin-up over window and door openings to catch overspray fallout from overhead ceiling work. Same zone as SF_DRYWALL_CEILING_NC_FINISH. Only for spray application.

protection_zones_analysis.conditional_protection_note: Floor protection varies by method: full_cover for spray, edge_only for brush. Wall upper band masking and opening covers are spray-only. Fixture covers always required. Key distinction from SF_WOOD_WALL_NC: wood wall masks the ceiling above (ceiling_line zone); wood ceiling masks the wall below (wall_upper_band zone). This is the inverse relationship.

adjacent_surfaces.notes: Drywall wall field directly below wood ceiling. Different finish — drywall wall paint (flat/eggshell) vs millwork ceiling enamel (satin/semi-gloss). Junction at wall-ceiling line. When spraying ceiling, wall must be masked at this junction (wall_upper_band zone).

Crown molding at ceiling-wall junction when present. May be same finish group (wood ceiling + crown both millwork enamel) or different finish group (ceiling painted white, crown stained). Crown handled by SF_TRIM_NC_PAINT (ITM_TRIM_CROWN). When crown is present, it provides the wall-ceiling junction transition.

Wood wall panels below ceiling in wood-paneled rooms (libraries, accent rooms). Often same finish group — both millwork enamel, same color/sheen. Wood wall handled by SF_WOOD_WALL_NC. When both surfaces are same finish, junction may not need any masking.

Adjacent drywall ceiling field where wood ceiling transitions to drywall ceiling within the same level. Different finish — wood ceiling enamel (satin/semi-gloss) meets drywall ceiling paint (flat). Transition typically at a beam or soffit edge.

adjacency_analysis.surface_reference: Surface_Vocabulary_Reference.md v1.0 — ceiling_field exists in Ceiling Surfaces section. wall_field, trim_crown, wall_panel verified. 'ceiling_panel' proposed as new surface_id for wood ceiling substrate (distinct from ceiling_field which is semantically drywall).
adjacency_analysis.key_finding: Wood ceiling is adjacent to the wall below (inverse of wood wall's relationship to ceiling above). The primary protection concern is overspray falling DOWN onto walls and floor, not UP onto ceiling. When wood ceiling and wood wall share a room (library/accent room), they are typically same finish group and can be sprayed in the same session. No edge work generated by this spec — transition surfaces (crown, baseboard) are separate specs.

affected_conditions.notes: Floor protection below ceiling work zone. Overhead spray drips land on floor. Finished floors need full protection. Subfloor may not need protection in NC. Ceiling spray creates MORE floor exposure than wall spray because overspray falls straight down over entire room.

affected_conditions.modifier_notes: occupied_sensitive triggers OCC_SENSITIVE modifier 1.30x on protection tasks per Modifier_Registry
affected_conditions.notes: Additional protection when occupied — furniture and belongings below ceiling work. Ceiling work drops debris (sanding dust, drips) onto everything below. More critical than wall work because gravity affects entire room, not just perimeter.

Temperature affects dry times, open time, and flow-out. Warm air rises — ceiling surfaces are typically warmer than walls, which can accelerate dry time and reduce open time for waterborne products. This is especially impactful for QT4+ waterborne alkyds that rely on extended open time for leveling. Hot conditions amplify this effect on overhead surfaces.

MDF edge sealing uses solvent-based products (shellac/oil-based) — adequate ventilation required. Spray application generates overspray requiring air movement. Poor ventilation extends dry times. Overhead spray creates more airborne particles than wall spray. Particularly relevant in enclosed rooms where wood ceilings are common.

affected_conditions.modifier_notes: Height modifier via PS_META.HEIGHT_BAND: H1=1.0x, H2=1.30x, H3=1.50x, H4=2.00x
affected_conditions.notes: ALL overhead work requires access equipment — unlike walls where standard height can be reached from floor. Standard 8 ft ceiling still needs a step ladder for overhead brush work. Scaffold or lift for taller ceilings. Access equipment setup/repositioning adds significant overhead to every task.

valid_input_states.rationale: Combined prime+paint spec. SS_BARE (uncoated MDF, FJP, or solid wood ceiling panels/boards) requires full primer coat — primer type driven by substrate. SS_PRIMED_FACTORY (standard NC — factory-primed MDF, FJP, or pre-primed boards) skips primer, lighter prep.

output_state.rationale: Output state varies by sheen configuration dimension. Satin is default for wood ceilings (softer appearance, minimizes reflection/glare from ceiling-mounted lighting).

adjacent_state_protection_analysis.rationale: Typical NC: walls often painted before ceiling detail work (walls are field painting, ceiling millwork is detail). When wall SS_PAINTED_*: masking required at upper wall band during spray. When wall unfinished: no protection needed. Note this is the INVERSE of wood wall spec which protects ceiling above.
If crown already painted, mask junction during ceiling work. Typically same finish group — usually painted in same session, so rarely needs protection.
Wood wall panels below ceiling — often same finish group, often painted in same session. If already finished, mask upper portion near ceiling during ceiling spray.

required_paintscope_keys.description: Total SF of wood ceiling surface (plank, beadboard, T&G, coffered panel+beam)
required_paintscope_keys.catalog_status: PROPOSED — no existing key covers wood ceiling surfaces. PS_SURFACE_SF.CEILING_FIELD is semantically for drywall ceilings. This is a distinct surface — wood substrate, fine finish doctrine, overhead methodology, different prep and production rates.

required_paintscope_keys.description: Full floor protection area below ceiling work zone (spray)
Perimeter floor protection area at ceiling work zone (brush)
Upper wall band masking SF near ceiling for overspray containment
Ceiling-mounted fixture count for masking (lights, fans, smoke detectors)
Height classification for modifier selection — ceiling height varies by room, determines access equipment

proposed_new_keys.description: Total SF of wood ceiling surface. For board styles (flat_plank, beadboard, T&G), includes board faces and joint detail. For coffered style, includes panel faces AND beam faces within the ceiling system — beams are integral, not separate items. Measured as total ceiling area covered by wood surface.
proposed_new_keys.justification: No existing key covers wood ceiling surfaces. PS_SURFACE_SF.CEILING_FIELD is semantically for drywall ceilings (used by SF_DRYWALL_CEILING_NC_PRIME / SF_DRYWALL_CEILING_NC_FINISH). This surface is semantically distinct — wood substrate, fine finish doctrine, overhead-specific methodology, different prep and production rates. Same rationale as PS_SURFACE_SF.WOOD_WALL for wood walls.

adjacency_notes.scope_impact: Wood ceiling meets wall field at wall-ceiling line. Different finish — ceiling enamel vs wall latex. This is the PRIMARY protection concern — spray overspray from ceiling falls/drifts down onto finished walls. Wall_upper_band masking zone addresses this.
adjacency_notes.nc_context: Typical NC: walls often painted before ceiling detail work (walls are field painting phase, wood ceiling is millwork detail phase).

adjacency_notes.scope_impact: When crown molding is present, it occupies the wall-ceiling junction and provides the physical transition. Crown is trim spec scope (SF_TRIM_NC_PAINT). When crown is present, the wall_upper_band masking zone may be partially handled by the crown installation.
adjacency_notes.nc_context: Crown and wood ceiling may be same or different finish groups. When same color, painted in same session.

adjacency_notes.scope_impact: In wood-paneled rooms (libraries, studies), wood ceiling meets wood wall at the ceiling-wall junction. Typically same finish group — painted in same session, possibly by same crew. Junction at wall-ceiling line. When same finish, minimal protection needed.
adjacency_notes.nc_context: Wood ceiling and wood wall are often combined in the same room and same session. Shared finish group, shared material system.

adjacency_notes.scope_impact: Internal edges within the coffered ceiling system — beam faces to panel fields, beam-to-beam corners, beam soffit edges. ALL within this spec's scope. Caulking at beam-to-panel junctions is a mandatory prep task for coffered style. Inside corners at beam/panel transitions require detail work.
adjacency_notes.nc_context: Internal assembly joints — caulked during prep phase. Coffered beams create multiple inside corners that slow production.

adjacency_notes.scope_impact: Internal edges within board-style ceilings — board-to-board joints (beadboard bead groove, T&G tight joint, flat_plank butt joint). ALL within this spec's scope. Joint detail drives ceiling_style complexity modifier. Caulking at board joints is a prep task (where applicable).
adjacency_notes.nc_context: Internal board joints — caulked during prep phase where applicable. Beadboard has the highest joint density.

relevant_findings.topic: Single SF item for entire wood ceiling surface
relevant_findings.finding: The wood ceiling surface (boards or panel+beam assembly) is measured as ONE item in SF. For coffered style, beam complexity is captured by the ceiling_style modifier (1.35x), not by splitting into separate items. For board styles (beadboard, T&G, flat_plank), joint detail complexity is captured by the ceiling_style modifier. This matches Millwork Doctrine §1.1 approach and parallels SF_WOOD_WALL_NC's single-item design.
relevant_findings.impact: Single ITM_WOOD_CEILING_PANEL with SF UOM. All production rates expressed in SF/hr.

relevant_findings.topic: Combined prime+paint spec — primer conditional on substrate_state
relevant_findings.finding: This spec includes both primer and finish coats, but primer is conditional. SS_BARE requires full primer coat (substrate-driven chemistry). SS_PRIMED_FACTORY skips primer — lighter prep only. Matches SF_WOOD_WALL_NC, SF_WAINSCOT_PANEL_NC, and SF_WINDOW_INT_NC pattern. Rationale: a wood ceiling is a self-contained surface with continuous finish — primer and paint flow continuously across the entire ceiling field in the same session.
relevant_findings.impact: Module structure must support both workflows. Prime module is conditional. Two variant round configs: with/without primer.

relevant_findings.topic: Substrate drives primer chemistry — 5 distinct primer paths (identical to wood wall)
relevant_findings.finding: MDF cut/routed edges: solvent-based sealer (Zinsser BIN Shellac, KILZ Original) — water-based causes irreversible fiber swelling. MDF faces: high-build latex (BM Enamel Underbody 217). FJP: stain-blocking primer MANDATORY (BM Prime Lock Plus). Solid wood softwood: standard primer-sealer (Zinsser Bulls Eye 1-2-3). Solid wood hardwood: tannin-blocking primer (BM Prime Lock Plus, SW Extreme Block). MDF requires TWO-STEP prime: edge seal (solvent) then face prime (latex). Identical primer chemistry matrix to SF_WOOD_WALL_NC and SF_WAINSCOT_PANEL_NC.
relevant_findings.impact: Materials Manager must include 5 substrate-driven primer systems. SOP must have substrate-conditional primer tasks. MDF edge sealing is a separate mandatory task before latex primer.

relevant_findings.topic: Ceiling style drives complexity modifier — 4 styles with overhead-specific considerations
relevant_findings.finding: Four ceiling styles with distinct production rate modifiers: flat_plank (1.0x — simple flat boards, easiest overhead surface), beadboard (1.15x — narrow boards ~3-4 inches wide with bead groove at each joint, high joint density overhead), tongue_and_groove (1.10x — interlocking boards with tight joints, similar to beadboard but wider boards/fewer joints), coffered (1.35x — grid of beams forming recessed panel bays, most complex: beam faces, panel fields, beam-to-panel junctions, inside corners, multiple orientation changes). These map to Millwork Doctrine §7.2 complexity categories.
relevant_findings.impact: ceiling_style is a configuration dimension driving production rate complexity modifier. Applied to all qt_scaled tasks.

relevant_findings.topic: ALL work is overhead — inherently slower base rates than wall work
relevant_findings.finding: Every task in this spec is performed overhead. This fundamentally changes base production rates compared to equivalent wall work. Key factors: (1) Physical strain — arms above head, neck strain, fatigue cycles shorter; (2) Gravity effects — drips fall onto worker and floor, sag risk on overhead horizontal surfaces, spray material fights gravity; (3) Equipment positioning — must position ladders/scaffold for overhead reach, more frequent repositioning; (4) Inspection difficulty — looking up vs straight ahead, angled light required to reveal defects overhead; (5) Sanding difficulty — overhead sanding is especially fatiguing, sanding dust falls onto worker. Typical overhead penalty: ~0.70-0.80x of equivalent wall rates (i.e., 20-30% slower).
relevant_findings.source: Brief Section 13; industry standard overhead work factors
relevant_findings.impact: Base production rates for ALL tasks must be inherently lower than SF_WOOD_WALL_NC equivalents. The height modifier then applies ON TOP of these reduced rates.

relevant_findings.topic: Height modifier applies ON TOP of overhead base rates
relevant_findings.finding: Room height determines access equipment requirements. The height modifier (MOD_HT via PS_META.HEIGHT_BAND) applies to production rate tasks on top of the already-reduced overhead base rates. H1=1.0x (8-9 ft standard ceiling — step ladder), H2=1.30x (9-12 ft — taller step ladder), H3=1.50x (13-17 ft — scaffold), H4=2.00x (18-24 ft — scaffold or lift). Combined example: a 14 ft wood ceiling at flat_plank is approximately 0.75 (overhead) × (1/1.5) (H3) = 0.50x the rate of a standard wall task. This is a KEY distinction from SF_WOOD_WALL_NC which shares the same height modifiers but starts from higher (wall-rate) baselines.
relevant_findings.impact: No height dimension in spec. Height modifier applied by estimation engine per room. Production rate tasks must declare height_band sensitivity. Base rates already factor in overhead penalty.

relevant_findings.topic: Coffered ceiling beams are IN SCOPE — integral to ceiling system
relevant_findings.finding: Coffered ceiling beams are included in this spec because: (1) beams and panels form a single integrated ceiling system painted together, (2) separating beams into SF_ARCH_ELEMENT_NC creates coordination complexity for no benefit, (3) the ceiling_style=coffered modifier (1.35x) captures the beam complexity. Standalone decorative beams (not part of a coffered grid) are EXCLUDED — routed to SF_ARCH_ELEMENT_NC. Coffered beam faces are partially vertical surfaces within the ceiling system, which means they have less overhead penalty than the horizontal panel fields — captured in the 1.35x modifier which accounts for the mixed-orientation complexity.
relevant_findings.impact: Coffered beam face painting is included. No separate ITM for beams. Ceiling_style=coffered modifier captures all beam-related complexity.

relevant_findings.topic: MDF edge sealing is a non-negotiable two-step process (identical to wood wall)
relevant_findings.finding: When substrate is MDF and substrate_state is SS_BARE, the SOP MUST include solvent-based edge sealing as a separate prep task BEFORE latex face primer. Water-based primer on raw MDF edges causes irreversible fiber swelling. This is the same constraint as in SF_WOOD_WALL_NC, SF_WAINSCOT_PANEL_NC, and SF_STAIR_RISER_NC — it is task-sequence critical, not just material selection. Overhead edge sealing is more difficult — sealer tends to run/drip from overhead edges due to gravity.
relevant_findings.impact: SOP must enforce edge seal before face prime for bare MDF. Two separate tasks in prime module.

relevant_findings.topic: QT2 not applicable — wood ceilings are prominent millwork
relevant_findings.finding: Per Millwork Doctrine §6 and Fine Finish Doctrine: wood ceilings are prominent, design-feature surfaces. QT2 is not applicable. Minimum quality tier is QT3. Wood ceilings are intentional architectural elements (libraries, great rooms, entries) — they are always prominent and visible.
relevant_findings.impact: Spec configuration_dimensions must exclude QT2. Only QT3, QT4, QT5 valid.

relevant_findings.topic: Finish material systems — reuse existing SYS_FF_ IDs
relevant_findings.finding: Same SYS_FF_ finish systems as SF_WOOD_WALL_NC, SF_TRIM_NC_PAINT, SF_WINDOW_INT_NC, SF_STAIR_RISER_NC, and SF_WAINSCOT_PANEL_NC. QT3: SYS_FF_STANDARD_ACRYLIC (100% acrylic enamel). QT4: SYS_FF_MODIFIED_URETHANE (waterborne alkyd). QT5: SYS_FF_PREMIUM (premium urethane enamel). Material systems are recommendations — contractor has discretion (RC-005). REUSE OVER CREATION — no new finish systems needed.
relevant_findings.impact: Reuse existing SYS_FF_ IDs. Same primer SYS_ IDs as wainscot and wood wall. No new material systems needed.

relevant_findings.topic: Interstage is universal at ALL quality tiers
relevant_findings.finding: Same pattern as all fine finish specs. Interstage runs after every coat except the final coat. Sanding discipline: QT3=spot sand only (nibs, rough spots), QT4=full 220 grit, QT5=thorough 220-320 grit. Rigid sanding block mandatory for defect removal (FFD §15.4.1). Overhead sanding is especially fatiguing — may need shorter work intervals. Sanding dust falls onto worker during overhead work.
relevant_findings.impact: Interstage module present at all QTs. Sanding discipline varies by QT. Overhead sanding penalty factored into interstage rates.

relevant_findings.topic: Spray technique differs for overhead surfaces
relevant_findings.finding: Wood ceiling spray technique differs from walls: (1) Spray gun angle — overhead spraying requires different arm position and spray fan orientation; (2) Gravity management — material must be applied in lighter coats to prevent sags and drips, as gravity pulls wet coating downward from overhead surfaces; (3) Coffered: panel fields first (broad overhead passes), then beam faces (vertical surfaces within the ceiling system — less overhead penalty for beam faces since they're vertical); (4) Board styles: sweep passes following board direction, maintain consistent distance. Beadboard narrow boards require more attention to groove detail. (5) Backroll is NOT standard for overhead wood ceiling — spray only for NC production (unlike wall spray_backroll).
relevant_findings.source: Brief Section 13; industry spray technique for overhead surfaces
relevant_findings.impact: Spray is default application method for NC production. Application_method values: spray, brush (no spray_backroll for overhead wood ceiling).

relevant_findings.topic: Fixture masking is ALWAYS required — ceiling fixtures are embedded in work surface
relevant_findings.finding: Unlike wall specs where ceiling fixtures are above the work surface, wood ceiling specs have fixtures EMBEDDED in the work surface. Ceiling-mounted lights, fans, smoke detectors, sprinkler heads are all within the ceiling plane being painted. Fixture masking is required regardless of application method (brush or spray). This is a mandatory binary task — same at all QTs.
relevant_findings.impact: fixture_covers zone is always-required (not method-conditional). Separate from wall_upper_band which is spray-only.

relevant_findings.topic: Sheen/QT gate — no tension with defaults
relevant_findings.finding: Brief sets QT3 default and satin default. These are compatible per FFD §4.1: satin at QT3+, semi-gloss at QT4+, gloss at QT5 only. No tension exists — QT3+satin is a valid combination. Same as SF_WOOD_WALL_NC. Wood ceilings typically use satin for a softer appearance and to minimize glare from ceiling-mounted lighting.
relevant_findings.impact: No runtime gate rejection. Satin default compatible with QT3 default.

relevant_findings.topic: Board joint caulking overhead is slower and messier than wall caulking
relevant_findings.finding: Same joint density patterns as wood wall, but caulking overhead is significantly slower. Gravity pulls caulk away from joints during application. For beadboard (highest joint density with narrow 3-4 inch boards), caulk labor is substantially higher overhead compared to wall equivalent. Caulk must be tooled quickly before sagging. Perimeter caulk at ceiling-to-wall junction is also an overhead task.
relevant_findings.impact: Caulk task rates must reflect overhead penalty. Beadboard has highest caulk labor due to high joint density + overhead penalty.

relevant_findings.finding: The existing surface_id 'ceiling_field' is semantically for drywall ceilings (used by SF_DRYWALL_CEILING_NC_PRIME and SF_DRYWALL_CEILING_NC_FINISH). Wood ceiling panels/boards are a different substrate type requiring different doctrine (Fine Finish vs standard wall/ceiling). Following the pattern where 'wall_panel' was created for wood walls (distinct from 'wall_field' for drywall walls), a new surface_id 'ceiling_panel' should be proposed for wood ceiling substrate.
relevant_findings.source: id_registry.json surface_ids; pattern from SF_WOOD_WALL_NC (wall_panel vs wall_field)
relevant_findings.impact: Propose 'ceiling_panel' as new surface_id. ITM_WOOD_CEILING_PANEL surface_ref should be 'ceiling_panel'. Adjacency primary_surface should be 'ceiling_panel'.

condition_drivers.notes: QT drives finish material system (recommendations), sheen restrictions, sanding between coats, inspection scrutiny. Does NOT drive primer selection (substrate-driven). Does NOT affect application quality baseline.

Spray is strongly preferred for overhead — faster, more ergonomic, better coverage on horizontal-downward surfaces. Brush for small areas, occupied spaces, or detail work on coffered beam profiles. Spray requires floor_full + wall_upper_band + fixture_covers + opening_cover_lightweight. Brush requires floor_perimeter + fixture_covers. Per FFD §15.1.1.

flat_plank=1.0x baseline, beadboard=1.15x (narrow board bead groove detail), tongue_and_groove=1.10x (tight joint), coffered=1.35x (beam+panel system, inside corners, multiple orientation changes). Modifiers from Millwork Doctrine §7.2 complexity categories adapted for ceiling. Beadboard and T&G are board styles. Flat_plank is simple board. Coffered is panel+beam assembly.
SS_BARE: full primer coat required (substrate-driven chemistry), heavier prep. SS_PRIMED_FACTORY: skip primer, scuff sand only. Standard NC delivery is factory-primed.
Sheen/QT gate per FFD §4.1: satin at QT3+, semi-gloss at QT4+, gloss at QT5 only. Satin is default (softer appearance, reduced glare from ceiling-mounted lighting).

quality_differences.qt3: SYS_FF_STANDARD_ACRYLIC — 100% acrylic enamel (ProClassic WB, Regal Select)
quality_differences.qt4: SYS_FF_MODIFIED_URETHANE — waterborne alkyd (BM Advance, SW Pro Industrial WB Alkyd)
quality_differences.qt5: SYS_FF_PREMIUM — premium urethane enamel (Emerald Urethane, Scuff-X)

quality_differences.qt3: Spot sand only — visible nibs, rough spots
quality_differences.qt4: Light full sand — 220 grit, entire surface for adhesion
quality_differences.qt5: Thorough full sand — 220-320 grit, uniform scratch pattern

quality_differences.qt3: Quick glance from floor — obvious defects only (overhead inspection is inherently less detailed from distance)
quality_differences.qt4: Systematic scan from step ladder — all visible defects marked
quality_differences.qt5: Lighted critical inspection from scaffold/ladder — zero tolerance (angled light to reveal overhead defects)
2-3 finish coats (3+ typical for brush per FFD §15.10.3)

quality_differences.qt3: Same baseline — no drips, sags, holidays, lap marks (NOT tiered). Overhead sag prevention is universal.
Fill obvious holes, functional caulk lines, light scuff sand
quality_differences.qt4: Fill all visible holes, smooth caulk lines, full sand 180-220
quality_differences.qt5: Fill every hole, perfect caulk, thorough sand 220+, uniform scratch

failure_modes.failure: MDF fiber swelling on cut/routed edges
failure_modes.cause: Applying water-based primer to raw MDF cut/routed edges before solvent-based sealer
failure_modes.prevention: ALWAYS seal MDF edges with shellac-based (Zinsser BIN) or oil-based (KILZ Original) sealer FIRST. Two-step prime process for bare MDF. Per Millwork_NC_Paint_Doctrine §2.1 and §4.1.
failure_modes.reversibility: Difficult — requires sanding back to substrate, fiber swelling is irreversible without aggressive sanding

failure_modes.cause: Using non-stain-blocking primer on bare finger-joint pine
failure_modes.prevention: ALWAYS use stain-blocking primer on bare FJP. BM Prime Lock Plus, BM Fresh Start oil-based, or Zinsser BIN Shellac. MANDATORY per Millwork Doctrine §2.2 and §4.1.
failure_modes.reversibility: Difficult — resin bleed re-emerges through multiple finish coats

failure_modes.cause: Using water-based primer without tannin-blocking properties on bare hardwood (oak, maple, cherry)
failure_modes.prevention: ALWAYS use tannin-blocking primer on bare hardwood. BM Prime Lock Plus, SW Extreme Block, or shellac-based primer.
failure_modes.reversibility: Difficult — tannin bleed re-emerges through multiple finish coats

failure_modes.failure: Overhead sags and drips on ceiling surface
failure_modes.cause: Over-application of paint on overhead horizontal surface — gravity pulls wet coating down, creating sags at board edges and drip accumulation at joints
failure_modes.prevention: Apply lighter coats overhead than on walls. Spray: maintain consistent distance and speed, avoid double-pass overlap. Brush: load brush lighter, tip carefully. Multiple thin coats better than one heavy coat. Monitor board edges and joints for accumulation during application.
failure_modes.reversibility: Addressable — sand between coats to level sags, recoat. More difficult overhead.

failure_modes.failure: Beadboard groove holidays — incomplete coverage in narrow bead grooves
failure_modes.cause: Spray passes too fast across narrow beadboard grooves, brush too wide for groove detail. Overhead angle makes groove bottoms harder to reach.
failure_modes.prevention: Spray technique: angle passes to reach groove bottoms, use appropriate tip size for groove penetration. Brush technique: size brush to groove width. Check all grooves for holidays before moving on. Overhead position makes holiday detection harder — use angled light.
failure_modes.reversibility: Easy — additional coat addresses holidays. Part of interstage inspection.

failure_modes.cause: Incomplete coverage in inside corners where beams meet panels — spray can't reach corners, brush misses recessed areas. Multiple orientation changes (horizontal panels to vertical beam faces).
failure_modes.prevention: Spray technique: panel fields first, then beam faces with HVLP or fine-finish tip for detail. Brush technique: work panel-to-beam sequence. Check all inside corners for holidays. Use angled light for overhead inspection.
failure_modes.reversibility: Easy — additional coat addresses holidays. Part of interstage inspection.

failure_modes.failure: Board groove fill — loss of groove definition on beadboard/T&G
failure_modes.cause: Excessive paint buildup in grooves, filling the groove profile and losing board definition. Gravity causes paint to pool in grooves on overhead surfaces.
failure_modes.prevention: Thin coats on board-style ceilings. Spray preferred — atomized application minimizes groove fill. If brushing, use brush sized to groove width. Avoid over-application. Extra vigilance overhead where gravity pools material in grooves.
failure_modes.reversibility: Moderate — requires careful sanding in grooves to restore definition, then recoat.

failure_modes.failure: Brush marks on flat plank ceiling areas
failure_modes.cause: Overworking waterborne product on large flat overhead surfaces, inadequate open time management. Warm air at ceiling level accelerates dry time.
failure_modes.prevention: Waterborne philosophy (FFD §15.3.1): Apply, tip once, walk away. Use quality brush with proper loading. Work in manageable sections. Large overhead areas amplify this risk. Warm air at ceiling level further reduces open time.
failure_modes.reversibility: Addressable — sand between coats with rigid block and recoat

failure_modes.failure: Caulk joint failure overhead — sagging during application
failure_modes.cause: Gravity pulls wet caulk out of overhead joints during application. Caulk sags and creates uneven joint lines.
failure_modes.prevention: Apply caulk in shorter beads overhead. Tool immediately after application to prevent sagging. Use thicker-consistency caulk formulation (not thin/runny). Support caulk gun at proper angle for overhead work.
failure_modes.reversibility: Easy — re-caulk affected areas. Part of normal prep.

failure_modes.failure: Sanding dust contamination — dust falls onto wet coat
failure_modes.cause: Overhead sanding between coats generates dust that falls onto the floor and any nearby wet surfaces. If not properly cleaned before next coat, trapped dust creates nibs.
failure_modes.prevention: Thorough tack-cloth wipe after sanding. Wait for airborne dust to settle before coating. Vacuum work area between coats. Wear appropriate PPE during overhead sanding.
failure_modes.reversibility: Easy — sand out nibs between coats.

notes_for_materials_manager.topic: Dual material system — substrate-driven primer, QT-driven finish (identical to wood wall)
notes_for_materials_manager.content: This spec has TWO independent material system layers: (1) Primer systems are substrate-driven (MDF edge seal + face prime, FJP stain-blocking, hardwood tannin-blocking, softwood standard). (2) Finish systems are QT-driven (SYS_FF_STANDARD_ACRYLIC, SYS_FF_MODIFIED_URETHANE, SYS_FF_PREMIUM). Same pattern as SF_WOOD_WALL_NC, SF_WAINSCOT_PANEL_NC, SF_STAIR_RISER_NC, and SF_WINDOW_INT_NC. All SYS_ IDs reused — no new material systems needed.

notes_for_materials_manager.topic: Primer selection by substrate — identical to wood wall and wainscot
notes_for_materials_manager.content: MDF cut/routed edges: Solvent-based sealer (SYS_PRIMER_MDF_SHELLAC — Zinsser BIN Shellac, KILZ Original). MDF factory faces: High-build latex (SYS_PRIMER_MDF_LATEX — BM Enamel Underbody 217, ProClassic Undercoater). FJP: Stain-blocking primer MANDATORY (SYS_PRIMER_POPLAR_STAINBLOCK — BM Prime Lock Plus, BM Fresh Start oil-based). Softwood: Standard primer-sealer (SYS_PRIMER_WOOD_STANDARD — Zinsser Bulls Eye 1-2-3, KILZ 2). Hardwood: Tannin-blocking primer (SYS_PRIMER_HARDWOOD_TANNINBLOCK — BM Prime Lock Plus, SW Extreme Block). Factory-primed: No primer needed.

notes_for_materials_manager.topic: Finish material systems — reuse from all fine finish specs
notes_for_materials_manager.content: Same SYS_FF_ finish systems as all other fine finish specs. Material systems are recommendations — contractor has discretion (RC-005). QT3: SYS_FF_STANDARD_ACRYLIC, QT4: SYS_FF_MODIFIED_URETHANE, QT5: SYS_FF_PREMIUM.

notes_for_materials_manager.topic: Caulk for board joints, beam-panel junctions, and perimeter
notes_for_materials_manager.content: Paintable acrylic latex caulk for: (1) board-to-board joints — beadboard bead groove, T&G joints (when caulked), flat_plank butt joints, (2) beam-to-panel junctions (coffered style), (3) ceiling-to-wall junction perimeter. Caulk quantity derived from ceiling SF — joint density varies by ceiling_style. Beadboard has highest joint density. Overhead caulking requires thicker-consistency caulk to resist sagging.

notes_for_materials_manager.topic: Coverage rates for wood ceiling SF
notes_for_materials_manager.content: Wood ceiling is measured directly in SF. Typical coverage: 350-450 SF/gal for finish coat on primed smooth surface. Coffered style may consume ~15% more material due to increased surface area from beam faces and inside corners. Beadboard/T&G groove detail increases material consumption slightly (~5-10%) due to paint in grooves. Overhead application may have slightly higher waste factor due to drips and gravity-related material loss.

notes_for_materials_manager.topic: Sanding consumables vary by tier — pole sander recommended for overhead
notes_for_materials_manager.content: QT3: 220 grit for spot sanding only. QT4: 220 grit for full surface. QT5: 220-320 grit for full surface. Rigid sanding blocks mandatory for defect removal (FFD §15.4.1). Flexible sanding sponge acceptable for beadboard/T&G grooves and coffered beam-panel inside corners. Pole sander strongly recommended for overhead field sanding to reduce worker fatigue.

notes_for_materials_manager.topic: Floor protection and wall masking materials
notes_for_materials_manager.content: Spray: Full floor coverage (canvas drop cloths or builder's paper) + upper wall band masking at ceiling-wall junction (masking paper 12-24 inches wide with tape line) + lightweight opening covers. Brush: Perimeter drop cloth runners. Fixture masking: tape + plastic bag or masking film over each ceiling fixture (always required). Materials consumption is higher than wood wall because floor_full covers entire room (not just perimeter).

Board-style ceilings (beadboard, T&G, flat_plank) have fastener holes from pneumatic nailing. Overhead spackle application is messier — spackle drips from putty knife. Use thicker-consistency lightweight spackle for overhead work. Overfill-sand-flush method per Materials_and_Consumables_Doctrine with HIGH waste factor. Same density patterns as wood wall but slower execution overhead.

notes_for_sop_librarian.topic: Module structure is combined prime+paint with single SF UOM
notes_for_sop_librarian.content: SETUP → PREP → [PRIME (conditional)] → FINISH_COAT_1 → INTERSTAGE → FINISH_COAT_2 → [INTERSTAGE → FINISH_COAT_3 at QT5 brush] → FINAL_INSPECT → CLEANUP. Prime module runs only when substrate_state = SS_BARE. Factory-primed substrates skip from prep to finish.

notes_for_sop_librarian.topic: No canonical painting sequence — single paintable item
notes_for_sop_librarian.content: Like SF_WOOD_WALL_NC, this spec has only ONE paintable item (ITM_WOOD_CEILING_PANEL, SF). No component-level sequencing required. Spray technique within the ceiling varies by ceiling_style: beadboard/T&G/flat_plank — sweep passes following board direction overhead; coffered — field panels first (broad overhead passes), then beam faces (vertical surfaces within ceiling system — less overhead penalty for beam faces).

notes_for_sop_librarian.topic: Prep tasks vary by substrate type (identical to wood wall)
notes_for_sop_librarian.content: Bare MDF: sand faces 220, clean dust, fill fastener holes, caulk joints, MDF edge seal (separate mandatory task). Bare FJP: light sand 150-180, clean, fill, caulk. Bare softwood: sand 150-180, clean, fill, caulk. Bare hardwood: sand 150-220, clean, fill, caulk. Factory-primed: scuff sand 150-180, clean, fill, caulk.

notes_for_sop_librarian.topic: Caulk joint types in prep — ceiling_style dependent
notes_for_sop_librarian.content: Board styles (beadboard, T&G, flat_plank): (1) board-to-board joints (bead groove, tight joint, or butt joint), (2) ceiling-to-wall junction perimeter. Coffered style: (1) beam-to-panel junctions (inside corners), (2) beam-to-beam joints at grid intersections, (3) ceiling-to-wall junction perimeter. All use paintable acrylic latex caulk. Caulk after fill and sand, before primer. Overhead caulking is slower — gravity pulls caulk from joints.

notes_for_sop_librarian.topic: MDF edge sealing is a separate mandatory task (identical to wood wall)
notes_for_sop_librarian.content: For bare MDF: edge seal (solvent-based) MUST run BEFORE latex primer. Two-step prime: (1) TSK_WDCL_SEAL_MDF_EDGES, (2) TSK_WDCL_PRIME_FACES. Water-based primers cause irreversible fiber swelling on MDF edges. Overhead edge sealing is more difficult — sealer tends to run/drip from overhead edges.

All task IDs use the WDCL context prefix per brief. Examples: TSK_WDCL_FLOOR_PROTECT, TSK_WDCL_WALL_MASK, TSK_WDCL_FIXTURE_MASK, TSK_WDCL_DUST_CLEAN, TSK_WDCL_SAND_PREP, TSK_WDCL_FILL_FASTENERS, TSK_WDCL_CAULK_JOINTS, TSK_WDCL_CAULK_PERIMETER, TSK_WDCL_SEAL_MDF_EDGES, TSK_WDCL_PRIME_FACES, TSK_WDCL_FINISH_COAT, TSK_WDCL_INTERSTAGE_SAND, TSK_WDCL_FINAL_INSPECT.

notes_for_sop_librarian.topic: Interstage is universal at ALL quality tiers
notes_for_sop_librarian.content: Interstage runs after every coat except the final coat. Tasks: clean area, inspect coat (from below with angled light), sand (spot or full per QT), patch/repair defects, sand patches, spot coat. Scrutiny level is qt_scaled. Overhead sanding is especially fatiguing — worker may need shorter work intervals.

notes_for_sop_librarian.topic: Wall masking and floor protection are setup tasks
notes_for_sop_librarian.content: When application_method=spray: (1) full floor protection, (2) wall upper band paper masking at ceiling-wall junction, (3) opening lightweight covers. When brush: (1) perimeter floor protection. Fixture masking is always required (binary task). Protection tasks belong in setup phase. Teardown tasks belong in cleanup phase.

At QT5 with brush application (especially semi-gloss/gloss), 3+ coats may be needed per FFD §15.10.3. Add additional FINISH_COAT + INTERSTAGE cycle as variant. Overhead brush application at QT5 gloss is the most demanding combination in this spec.

notes_for_sop_librarian.topic: Height impacts every task — ALL work is overhead
notes_for_sop_librarian.content: Unlike wood wall (where only H2+ requires access equipment), ALL ceiling tasks require overhead positioning. Even standard 8 ft ceilings need step ladders for brush work. Production rate tasks must be height-band sensitive — estimation engine applies MOD_HT per room. At H2+ heights, scaffolding or lifts are required, adding setup/repositioning time.

notes_for_estimation_engineer.topic: SF-based production rates with overhead penalty
notes_for_estimation_engineer.content: All tasks use SF as the primary UOM. Production rates expressed in SF/hr. Wood ceiling SF directly from PaintScope input. ALL rates must reflect overhead work penalty — base rates ~0.70-0.80x of equivalent SF_WOOD_WALL_NC rates.

notes_for_estimation_engineer.topic: Production rate estimates — overhead-adjusted from wood wall rates
notes_for_estimation_engineer.content: Base rates derived from SF_WOOD_WALL_NC rates with overhead penalty applied: Spray finish coat ~105-160 SF/hr for flat_plank at QT3 (vs ~150-200 for wood wall). Brush finish coat ~42-64 SF/hr for flat_plank at QT3 (vs ~60-80 for wood wall). Overhead penalty is ~0.70-0.80x applied to all task types. These are starting estimates — field validation recommended.

flat_plank=1.0x baseline, beadboard=1.15x (narrow board bead groove detail, many joints), tongue_and_groove=1.10x (tight joint detail), coffered=1.35x (beam+panel system, inside corners, multiple orientation changes). Apply to all qt_scaled tasks. Modifiers from Millwork Doctrine §7.2 adapted for ceiling.

notes_for_estimation_engineer.topic: Height modifier — varies per room, ON TOP of overhead base rates
notes_for_estimation_engineer.content: Ceiling height varies by room: H1=1.0x (8-9 ft, step ladder), H2=1.30x (9-12 ft, taller ladder), H3=1.50x (13-17 ft, scaffold), H4=2.00x (18-24 ft, scaffold/lift). Applied by estimation engine via PS_META.HEIGHT_BAND per room. These modifiers apply ON TOP of already-reduced overhead base rates. Combined effect example: 14 ft coffered ceiling = overhead_base × (1/1.5) × 1.35 = very slow production.

QT3=1.00, QT4=1.30, QT5=1.50. Apply to inspection, repair, and sanding tasks. Do NOT apply to application rate — application quality is the same at all tiers. Overhead inspection is inherently slower at all tiers — angled light needed, looking up.

Spray is significantly faster than brush for overhead work (~2.5-3x for flat_plank). The overhead penalty is LESS severe for spray than brush — spray ergonomics are better overhead (spray gun vs brush/roller above head). Coffered beam faces are partially vertical, reducing overhead penalty for that portion of the work.

Wood ceiling area varies significantly between rooms (small accent ceiling 40 SF vs great room ceiling 300+ SF). Interstage tasks must use SF as UOM — same rationale as SF_WOOD_WALL_NC and SF_WAINSCOT_PANEL_NC. Overhead interstage sanding is especially slow due to fatigue.

inherited_research_corrections.title: Do not specify dry times in specs
inherited_research_corrections.impact: No dry time references in materials or sop_modules — refer to PDS

inherited_research_corrections.title: Material systems are recommendations, not mandates
inherited_research_corrections.impact: Finish material systems are QT-driven recommendations — contractor has discretion

inherited_research_corrections.title: Advance is waterborne alkyd; Emerald Urethane is acrylic-urethane enamel

assumptions.value: 0.70-0.80x of equivalent wall production rates for all overhead tasks
assumptions.source: Brief Section 13 — industry standard overhead work factors
assumptions.note: No doctrine provides an explicit overhead penalty factor for ceiling work. Brief provides estimated range (0.70-0.80x) based on industry standard. Field validation recommended. The penalty is BAKED INTO base rates, not applied as a separate modifier.

assumptions.value: Spray finish coat ~105-160 SF/hr for flat_plank at QT3 (derived from wood wall 150-200 × 0.70-0.80)
assumptions.source: Derived from SF_WOOD_WALL_NC rates with overhead penalty
assumptions.note: No doctrine provides wood ceiling-specific SF production rates. Rates derived from wood wall rates with overhead penalty applied.

assumptions.value: Brush finish coat ~42-64 SF/hr for flat_plank at QT3 (derived from wood wall 60-80 × 0.70-0.80)
assumptions.source: Derived from SF_WOOD_WALL_NC rates with overhead penalty
assumptions.note: No doctrine provides wood ceiling-specific brush SF rates. Overhead brush work is more fatiguing than overhead spray — overhead penalty may be closer to 0.70x for brush.

assumptions.value: 1.15x complexity modifier for beadboard ceiling (matches shiplap wall modifier)
assumptions.note: Millwork Doctrine §7.2 does not explicitly list beadboard ceiling modifier. 1.15x matches shiplap wall modifier — beadboard has similar high joint density with narrow boards. Reasonable adaptation.

Millwork Doctrine §7.2 does not explicitly list coffered ceiling modifier. 1.35x is higher than library_panel wall (1.25x) because coffered adds beam faces (multiple orientation changes) and inside corners. Reasonable estimate — may need field validation.

assumptions.value: Proposed new surface_id 'ceiling_panel' for wood ceiling substrate
assumptions.source: Pattern from wall_panel (wood wall) vs wall_field (drywall wall)
assumptions.note: Surface_Vocabulary_Reference.md does not include 'ceiling_panel'. Proposed based on the pattern where wood substrates get distinct surface IDs (wall_panel, wainscot_panel) separate from their drywall equivalents (wall_field, ceiling_field).

uncertainties.description: No existing PaintScope key covers wood ceiling surfaces. PS_SURFACE_SF.CEILING_FIELD is for drywall. Proposed PS_SURFACE_SF.WOOD_CEILING as a new key.
uncertainties.current_approach: Proposed as new key in proposed_new_keys. Proceeding with assumption it will be activated.

uncertainties.description: The overhead penalty (0.70-0.80x) is a range. The exact factor depends on task type — spray has less overhead penalty than brush (spray ergonomics are better overhead). Sanding overhead is more fatiguing than sanding walls. The exact factor for each task type should be validated with field data.
uncertainties.current_approach: Using 0.75x as midpoint for all tasks. Estimation Engineer may differentiate by task type.

uncertainties.topic: Coffered beam face material consumption increase
uncertainties.description: Coffered beams add surface area (beam faces, soffits) that is not captured in the flat ceiling SF measurement. Actual increase depends on beam dimensions and grid density. Estimated ~15% more material consumption for coffered vs flat_plank.
uncertainties.current_approach: Flagged for Materials Manager to factor into coverage rates for coffered style.

uncertainties.topic: Height modifier interaction with overhead base rates
uncertainties.description: The overhead penalty is baked into base rates. The height modifier applies on top. At H3/H4, the combined effect may be very severe (e.g., 0.75 × 1/2.0 = 0.375x of wall rate for H4). This extreme slowdown may not be accurate for all task types — scaffold/lift may actually improve overhead reach compared to ladder. Field validation needed for H3+ ceiling work.
uncertainties.current_approach: Standard multiplicative stacking per doctrine. No special interaction handling.

uncertainties.description: Proposed 'ceiling_panel' as new surface_id following the wall_panel pattern. The brief uses 'ceiling_field' in adjacency declarations, which may need updating to 'ceiling_panel' for the primary surface. The Registry Resolver should resolve this.
uncertainties.current_approach: Research proposes 'ceiling_panel'. Resolver will determine final surface_id.
